name: Apollo
tagline: Facebook's Raft-replicated, sharded C++ data store shown at QCon 2014; never released or open-sourced.
description: Apollo was a distributed database that Facebook engineer Jeff Johnson presented at QCon New York in June 2014. Data was split into shards, each replicated with a Raft-based quorum protocol, and stored by default in RocksDB (MySQL was being tried as an alternative engine). Instead of a fixed document or key-value model it exposed atomic operations on data structures such as maps, queues, trees and key-value pairs, with read/write calls guarded by preconditions, and 'fault-tolerant state machines' handled cross-shard transactions, migration and load balancing. It was written in C++11 on Thrift 2 and targeted low-latency online storage, possible memcached replacements and reliable outbound message queues. It was not in production at the time, Facebook never open-sourced it, and nothing further was published, so it survives only as an early example of Raft-per-shard design.
statusNote: Internal Facebook project presented in 2014; never released or open-sourced, with no public updates since.

scale.notes: Designed for thousands of shards, from three servers up to thousands, and datasets from megabytes to 10+ PB; never documented in production.

strengths: Early public example of per-shard Raft replication at internet scale
Atomic conditional operations on rich data structures, not just opaque values
Storage-agnostic design with RocksDB as the primary engine
weaknesses: Never released; no code, documentation or users outside Facebook
Only described in a single 2014 conference talk and its write-ups
useCases: Historical reference for Raft-per-shard database design
Background reading on Facebook's storage evolution
notIdealFor: Any real deployment: the software is not available
